title: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26 — Duty to Disclose; General Provisions Governing Discovery, including the Rule 26(g) certification (rule text with Advisory Committee Notes)
pub: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
author: Advisory Committee on Civil Rules

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Rule 26 provides an analogous framework of case-specific proportionality, informed planning, reasonable inquiry and professional accountability for e-discovery. However, it does not address generative AI, jagged capability, task-level gains or human–AI work allocation, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

The rule simply requires that the attorney make a reasonable inquiry into the factual basis of his response, request, or objection.

kp.k: Discovery signatures certify reasonable inquiry and responsible conduct
kp.d: Rule 26(g) requires an attorney of record, or an unrepresented party, to sign initial and pretrial disclosures and discovery requests, responses, and objections. The certification rests on reasonable inquiry: disclosures must be complete and correct when made, while discovery demands and responses must have legal justification, avoid improper purposes, and avoid unreasonable burdens or expense. This is a discovery accountability standard, not an express rule about AI.
qs: By signing, an attorney or party certifies that to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief formed after a reasonable inquiry:
with respect to a disclosure, it is complete and correct as of the time it is made;

The subdivision provides a deterrent to both excessive discovery and evasion by imposing a certification requirement that obliges each attorney to stop and think about the legitimacy of a discovery request, a response thereto, or an objection.

kp.k: Reasonable inquiry is objective, contextual, not absolute assurance
kp.d: The 1983 Notes explain that reasonable inquiry depends on the investigation and conclusions being objectively reasonable in the circumstances. Reliance on clients and other counsel is permissible when appropriate, with courts judging the totality of circumstances. Certification of discovery responses concerns reasonable efforts to secure responsive information, not a guarantee that clients' factual answers are truthful.
qs: The duty to make a “reasonable inquiry” is satisfied if the investigation undertaken by the attorney and the conclusions drawn therefrom are reasonable under the circumstances.
In making the inquiry, the attorney may rely on assertions by the client and on communications with other counsel in the case as long as that reliance is appropriate under the circumstances.
Rule 26(g) does not require the signing attorney to certify the truthfulness of the client's factual responses to a discovery request.

Rather, the signature certifies that the lawyer has made a reasonable effort to assure that the client has provided all the information and documents available to him that are responsive to the discovery demand.

kp.k: Improper certification requires sanctions absent substantial justification
kp.d: Rule 26(g)(3) requires an appropriate sanction for certification violations without substantial justification, potentially against the signer, the represented party, or both. Recoverable expenses may include attorney fees caused by the violation. The 1983 Notes frame sanctions as deterrence, leave their nature to judicial discretion, and require due process; their projected reduction of abuse is a policy premise rather than a demonstrated outcome.
qs: If a certification violates this rule without substantial justification, the court, on motion or on its own, must impose an appropriate sanction on the signer, the party on whose behalf the signer was acting, or both.
The sanction may include an order to pay the reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, caused by the violation.
Thus the premise of Rule 26(g) is that imposing sanctions on attorneys who fail to meet the rule's standards will significantly reduce abuse by imposing disadvantages therefor.
The sanctioning process must comport with due process requirements.

kp.k: Proportionality defines discovery scope and shared responsibility
kp.d: The 2015 amendment places proportionality within the definition of discoverable nonprivileged matter relevant to claims or defenses. Factors include the importance of issues, monetary stakes, relative information access, resources, usefulness, and burdens versus benefits. The Notes connect this standard to Rule 26(g), reject boilerplate proportionality objections, and clarify that requesting parties do not bear every proportionality burden.
qs: This change reinforces the Rule 26(g) obligation of the parties to consider these factors in making discovery requests, responses, or objections.

Restoring the proportionality calculation to Rule 26(b)(1) does not change the existing responsibilities of the court and the parties to consider proportionality, and the change does not place on the party seeking discovery the burden of addressing all proportionality considerations.
Nor is the change intended to permit the opposing party to refuse discovery simply by making a boilerplate objection that it is not proportional.
The parties and the court have a collective responsibility to consider the proportionality of all discovery and consider it in resolving discovery disputes.

kp.k: Reliable search technology can alter discovery burden assessments
kp.d: The 2006 Notes recognize that electronic systems can make information easier to locate and retrieve, while other sources remain costly to access. The 2015 Notes recommend realistic burden assessments that consider reliable computer-based search methods as they develop, especially for large information volumes. The document discusses electronic search generally, without specifying generative AI, measured productivity improvements, or workforce displacement.
qs: Electronic storage systems often make it easier to locate and retrieve information.
These advantages are properly taken into account in determining the reasonable scope of discovery in a particular case.
Computer-based methods of searching such information continue to develop, particularly for cases involving large volumes of electronically stored information.
Courts and parties should be willing to consider the opportunities for reducing the burden or expense of discovery as reliable means of searching electronically stored information become available.

kp.k: Electronic discovery distinguishes accessibility from preservation and production
kp.d: Rule 26(b)(2)(B) permits identification of electronic sources as not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost; the responding party must substantiate that position when challenged. Good cause can nonetheless justify ordered discovery with conditions. The 2006 Notes contemplate sampling and focused discovery to test accessibility and value, and emphasize that inaccessible-source identification does not itself discharge preservation duties.
qs: A party need not provide discovery of electronically stored information from sources that the party identifies as not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost.
If that showing is made, the court may nonetheless order discovery from such sources if the requesting party shows good cause, considering the limitations of Rule 26(b)(2)(C).
A party's identification of sources of electronically stored information as not reasonably accessible does not relieve the party of its common-law or statutory duties to preserve evidence.

In such cases, the parties may need some focused discovery, which may include sampling of the sources, to learn more about what burdens and costs are involved in accessing the information, what the information consists of, and how valuable it is for the litigation in light of information that can be obtained by exhausting other opportunities for discovery.

kp.k: Information asymmetry and public values qualify cost constraints
kp.d: The 2015 Notes explain that discovery burdens may properly fall more heavily on parties holding more information. They reject treating monetary stakes or wealth as decisive: litigation with little or no monetary relief may vindicate important public or personal values, and resources neither eliminate discovery duties nor justify unlimited demands. These are qualifications on proportionality, not findings about enterprise savings or AI access to justice.
qs: In practice these circumstances often mean that the burden of responding to discovery lies heavier on the party who has more information, and properly so.
Many other substantive areas also may involve litigation that seeks relatively small amounts of money, or no money at all, but that seeks to vindicate vitally important personal or public values.
So too, consideration of the parties’ resources does not foreclose discovery requests addressed to an impecunious party, nor justify unlimited discovery requests addressed to a wealthy party.

kp.k: Cost allocation remains exceptional rather than presumptively shifted
kp.d: The 2015 amendment expressly recognizes protective orders allocating discovery expenses but does not endorse routine cost shifting. The 2006 Notes also explain that a requesting party's willingness to pay access costs does not resolve the producing party's separate burdens of relevance and privilege review.
qs: Recognizing the authority does not imply that cost-shifting should become a common practice.
Courts and parties should continue to assume that a responding party ordinarily bears the costs of responding.
But the producing party's burdens in reviewing the information for relevance and privilege may weigh against permitting the requested discovery.

kp.k: Electronic discovery requires technical preparation by counsel
kp.d: The 2006 Notes recommend that counsel understand clients' information systems before discovery planning and consider assistance from individuals with specialized systems knowledge. Early planning should address searchable sources, production formats, accessibility, and preservation. Preservation must balance evidentiary needs against ongoing operations rather than automatically halt computer activity.
qs: It may be important for the parties to discuss those systems, and accordingly important for counsel to become familiar with those systems before the conference.
In appropriate cases identification of, and early discovery from, individuals with special knowledge of a party's computer systems may be helpful.
The parties’ discussion should pay particular attention to the balance between the competing needs to preserve relevant evidence and to continue routine operations critical to ongoing activities.
Complete or broad cessation of a party's routine computer operations could paralyze the party's activities.

kp.k: Privilege review creates substantial electronic discovery costs
kp.d: The 2006 Notes report that privilege-waiver risks and preventive review increase discovery cost and delay, intensified by electronic volume, informal communications, embedded edits, and metadata. They describe quick-peek and clawback arrangements as potentially economical responses, while distinguishing the post-production claims procedure from substantive determinations of waiver.
qs: The Committee has repeatedly been advised that the risk of privilege waiver, and the work necessary to avoid it, add to the costs and delay of discovery.

The volume of such data, and the informality that attends use of e-mail and some other types of electronically stored information, may make privilege determinations more difficult, and privilege review correspondingly more expensive and time consuming.

Although these agreements may not be appropriate for all cases, in certain cases they can facilitate prompt and economical discovery by reducing delay before the discovering party obtains access to documents, and by reducing the cost and burden of review by the producing party.
Rule 26(b)(5)(B) does not address whether the privilege or protection that is asserted after production was waived by the production.

kp.k: 2025 amendments encourage tailored, early privilege-log planning
kp.d: Although the supplied title dates the source to 2015, its text includes 2025 amendments and Notes. Those Notes direct early planning about the timing and method of describing withheld materials, emphasizing case-specific flexibility rather than a uniform approach. Rolling production and descriptions can identify disputes before discovery closes. These are reform objectives and recommendations, not measured results.
qs: Compliance with Rule 26(b)(5)(A) can involve very large burdens for all parties.
This amendment directs the parties to address the question of how they will comply with Rule 26(b)(5)(A) in their discovery plan, and report to the court about this topic.
No one-size-fits-all approach would actually be suitable in all cases.
Often it will be valuable to provide for “rolling” production of materials and an appropriate description of the nature of the withheld material.

kp.k: Discovery exposure can distort expert staffing and collaboration
kp.d: The 2010 Notes report that broad discovery of expert drafts and attorney-expert communications increased costs, encouraged separate consulting and testifying experts, and inhibited effective collaboration. The amendments protect drafts and specified attorney-expert communications while preserving discovery of opinions and their bases. Exceptions cover compensation, attorney-provided facts or data considered, and attorney-provided assumptions relied upon; the communications protection is limited to experts required to provide reports.
qs: The Committee has been told repeatedly that routine discovery into attorney-expert communications and draft reports has had undesirable effects. Costs have risen.

Attorneys may employ two sets of experts — one for purposes of consultation and another to testify at trial — because disclosure of their collaborative interactions with expert consultants would reveal their most sensitive and confidential case analyses.

At the same time, attorneys often feel compelled to adopt a guarded attitude toward their interaction with testifying experts that impedes effective communication, and experts adopt strategies that protect against discovery but also interfere with their work.
Rules 26(b)(4)(B) and (C) do not impede discovery about the opinions to be offered by the expert or the development, foundation, or basis of those opinions.

kp.k: Work-product protection extends beyond lawyers' preparatory work
kp.d: Rule 26(b)(3) ordinarily protects litigation-preparation documents and tangible things prepared by or for parties and their representatives, not merely lawyers. Discovery requires otherwise discoverable material, substantial need, and inability to obtain its substantial equivalent without undue hardship, with protection for mental impressions and legal theories. The 1970 Notes distinguish this from ordinary business records and explain the aim of preserving independent preparation.
qs: Subdivision (b)(3) reflects the trend of the cases by requiring a special showing, not merely as to materials prepared by an attorney, but also as to materials prepared in anticipation of litigation or preparation for trial by or for a party or any representative acting on his behalf.

Materials assembled in the ordinary course of business, or pursuant to public requirements unrelated to litigation, or for other nonlitigation purposes are not under the qualified immunity provided by this subdivision.

On the other hand, the requirement of a special showing for discovery of trial preparation materials reflects the view that each side's informal evaluation of its case should be protected, that each side should be encouraged to prepare independently, and that one side should not automatically have the benefit of the detailed preparatory work of the other side.

kp.k: Disclosure obligations combine bounded inquiry with timely correction
kp.d: Rule 26 requires initial disclosures based on reasonably available information despite incomplete investigation or another party's noncompliance. The 2000 Notes narrow witness and document disclosure to material the party may use, superseding the broader 1993 approach. Rule 26(e) requires timely correction of materially incomplete or incorrect disclosures and specified discovery responses unless the information has otherwise been made known. Initial inquiry is therefore bounded, but later correction remains required.
qs: A party must make its initial disclosures based on the information then reasonably available to it.

A party is not excused from making its disclosures because it has not fully investigated the case or because it challenges the sufficiency of another party's disclosures or because another party has not made its disclosures.
A party is no longer obligated to disclose witnesses or documents, whether favorable or unfavorable, that it does not intend to use.
The obligation to supplement disclosures and discovery responses applies whenever a party learns that its prior disclosures or responses are in some material respect incomplete or incorrect.

kp.k: Adversarial incentives limit discovery's capacity for self-regulation
kp.d: The 1983 Notes identify excessive demands, evasive responses, and tactical use of discovery as sources of disproportionate expense and delay. The 2015 Notes say electronic discovery intensified the earlier information explosion and reiterate the need for close judicial involvement when cooperative party management fails. This is the Committee's institutional rationale for oversight, not evidence of an AI-specific market effect.
qs: Thus the spirit of the rules is violated when advocates attempt to use discovery tools as tactical weapons rather than to expose the facts and illuminate the issues by overuse of discovery or unnecessary use of defensive weapons or evasive responses.
All of this results in excessively costly and time-consuming activities that are disproportionate to the nature of the case, the amount involved, or the issues or values at stake.
What seemed an explosion in 1993 has been exacerbated by the advent of e-discovery.

But there will be important occasions for judicial management, both when the parties are legitimately unable to resolve important differences and when the parties fall short of effective, cooperative management on their own.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no explicit AI-specific claim or prediction. Its closest technology-related claim is that developing computer-based search methods offer opportunities to reduce discovery burdens and expense.
pts.d: The Advisory Committee's 2015 Notes state that computer-based methods for searching electronically stored information continue to develop and recommend considering cost-reduction opportunities as reliable methods become available. The 2006 Notes also state that electronic storage systems often make information easier to locate and retrieve. Neither passage identifies these methods as AI or predicts changes to legal employment, firm structures, or legal markets. Rule 26(g)'s reasonable-inquiry certification is a general discovery obligation, not an express claim about verification of AI output.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The search-efficiency claim is offered as Advisory Committee guidance, without quantified supporting evidence.
pts.d: The relevant 2006 and 2015 passages provide institutional observations and procedural guidance, not a study of search performance, a measured cost saving, or an AI benchmark. Historical studies and cases elsewhere in the document concern discovery practice and reform; they are not presented as empirical validation of AI or of the specific search-efficiency claim.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2015 claim is open-ended and conditional on reliable search methods becoming available; efficiencies remain case-specific.
pts.d: The Committee describes ongoing technological development without specifying an adoption deadline or forecasting the magnitude of savings. Its recommendation particularly concerns large volumes of electronically stored information. The 2006 Notes qualify the advantages of electronic storage by acknowledging that some sources remain costly or burdensome to access. Although the document heading gives 2015, the supplied compilation also includes amendments and Notes from 2025; the search-method claim belongs specifically to the 2015 Notes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Courts and litigating parties are the identified audiences; the potential effect is less burdensome or expensive electronic discovery.
pts.d: The recommendation addresses courts and parties determining realistic discovery burdens and proportionality, especially in information-heavy litigation. Responding parties ordinarily bear response costs, while requesting parties depend on access to discoverable information. The source does not identify AI vendors, particular law-firm segments, or lawyer roles as beneficiaries or displacement targets.
